Western Relocation Atlas

Eleven-state screen · home values as of August 2026

Western Relocation Atlas

Every census tract in the Mountain West, Washington, Oregon and California, scored on seven criteria, plus five optional ones, and grouped into 148 areas. Of 15,188 populated tracts, 10,172 pass the budget and airport filters.

The WestWashingtonOregonCaliforniaMontanaIdahoWyomingColoradoUtahNevadaArizonaNew MexicoMethod

The West at a glance

  • Seven criteria, weighted your way. Live music; mountains; parks and shore; peace and quiet; schools; climate risk to mid-century; access to a walkable core. To start, mountains count double parks and the two together count the same as each of the others; walkable core counts two-thirds as much. Five more start at zero, so they change nothing until you raise them: affordability (cheaper scores higher), hands-on K–8 schools, play-based pre-K, learning growth and tree cover. Their table columns appear once you weight them.
  • Scores are percentiles. Each criterion is ranked among all 15,188 tracts, 100 being best; Walkable core is the exception, shown as access out of 100. A neighborhood’s score is the weighted average of the criteria you weight.
  • An area’s score is its three best neighborhoods. So a metro can lead on a handful of streets while most of it scores lower.
  • Two filters. A typical home value of $300k to $950k, and an airport with daily airline service within about 100 km.
  • Walkable core means somewhere to get to. How close home is to a walkable town centre (full credit within about a 20-minute bike ride, fading out by about a 10–15 minute drive), scaled by the centre’s size, so a big downtown counts more than a small main street. Your own street doesn’t need to be walkable. Set how much a small main street counts with Small-core credit in Weights.
  • Every larger area has a neighborhood map. Click an underlined area name, or its dot on a map, to see every neighborhood in the area outlined and shaded by your weights.

Your weights

    Set what matters to you. Move a slider and every table, state summary and map on this page is recalculated from all 15,188 neighborhoods.

    • The percentage is each criterion’s share of the score. A slider at zero leaves that criterion out.
    • Drag a row by its handle to change the column order in every table. “Weights from order” turns that order into weights from 12 down to 1.
    • ▲ and ▼ beside a rank show how far the area has moved from its place at the original weights.
    • The Weights button in the bar above opens this panel from anywhere on the page, and every enlarged map has the same button, so you can watch the map change as you adjust. Your setting is kept in this browser where storage is allowed.

    Top twenty areas

    WA

    Washington

    • Pattern. Climate is the strength (88th percentile on average). Mountains are the weakness west of the Cascades, typically 23 km away.
    • East of the Cascades. The Tri-Cities, Yakima and Othello have almost no live music and heavy smoke.
    • Caveat. Wind comes from only six weather stations.

    Areas that pass both filters

    OR

    Oregon

    • Weak spot. Smoke. Eugene and Grants Pass have the worst readings in the screen, driven by the 2020 and 2022 fires. West of the Cascades the mountains are also 20–30 km away.
    • Caveats. Coast readings (Newport, Astoria) are borrowed from valley monitors 90 km away, so they are too high. There is no 2025 school data for Oregon.

    Areas that pass both filters

    CA

    California

    • In-budget weak spots. Schools: the typical in-budget neighborhood is 1.3 grades below the national average. Air: twice the ozone days of other states and a third more smoke and haze. Heat: most in-budget housing is inland.
    • Central Valley. Merced, Modesto, Bakersfield, Stockton and Fresno mostly face 80–125 very hot days by the 2050s.
    • Caveats. The climate score counts California’s rainless summer as dry-spell risk; that costs coastal areas such as Los Angeles a number of places. Central Valley heat estimates probably run 20–40 days high.

    Areas that pass both filters

    MT

    Montana

    • Pattern. Strong on schools, climate, quiet and mountains. Live music and walkable cores drop off sharply outside Missoula, Bozeman, Kalispell and Helena. Billings and Great Falls are far from mountains, with few venues.
    • Caveat. Bozeman’s air reading comes from monitors over 100 km away. Missoula and Bozeman both rely on regional airports.

    Areas that pass both filters

    ID

    Idaho

    • Pattern. Boise is near the top on music and mountains but only 35th percentile on climate (56 very hot days, smoke).
    • Snake River Plain. Twin Falls and Wendell are about 40 km from mountains, with below-average schools.

    Areas that pass both filters

    WY

    Wyoming

    • Pattern. Casper’s 12 mph average wind puts it in the 32nd percentile for quiet.
    • Caveat. Wind data covers only four Wyoming stations.

    Areas that pass both filters

    CO

    Colorado

    • Weak spots. Quiet (41st percentile: wind and big-metro density) and Front Range ozone: Boulder 15 days a year, Denver 11.
    • Caveat. Colorado’s 2025 school figures are estimated from state tests.

    Areas that pass both filters

    UT

    Utah

    • Pattern. The closest mountains of any state, typically 6 km. Quiet and air are the weak spots: 9 ozone days a year and winter haze in Salt Lake. St. George faces 113 very hot days by the 2050s.
    • Caveat. Wind for the whole Wasatch Front comes from one station.

    Areas that pass both filters

    NV

    Nevada

    • Pattern. Good on music and mountains. Weak on schools, quiet and heat: 130 very hot days for the typical neighborhood. Reno has heavy smoke.

    Areas that pass both filters

    AZ

    Arizona

    • Pattern. The weakest climate score of any state (24th percentile). Phoenix faces 163 very hot days and 15 ozone days a year. Flagstaff is strong on mountains and quiet, with schools half a grade below average.
    • Caveat. The mountain measure underrates Phoenix: its desert preserves are too small to register on a 4 km grid.

    Areas that pass both filters

    NM

    New Mexico

    • Pattern. Good music and mountains around Santa Fe and Albuquerque. Schools are the drag, typically 0.9 grades below average.
    • Caveat. Los Alamos has the best schools here (+1.7 grades), but the town-centre rule misses its downtown, so its walkable-core score is understated.

    Method and limits

    • This is a first-pass screen. It uses region-wide stand-ins for the measures in the neighborhood study, so it is good for finding candidates and less good for ranking streets within a city.
    • A neighborhood is a 2010 census tract1, and “home” is the tract’s centre of population2.
    • Weights apply to the twelve criteria. The mix inside a criterion (the four parts of climate, distance and size in the walkable core) and the two filters are fixed.
    • Music: a list of about 270 venues compiled by hand for this study, with jazz rooms weighted higher and small-market rooms lower.
    • Mountains: distance from home to terrain standing 300–500 m higher, on a 4 km elevation grid3. Narrow valleys and small desert ranges are underrated.
    • Parks and shore: the share of land within 1.5 km of home that is park or protected open space4, plus a bonus for salt-water shore within 3 km5. The inner bays of San Francisco Bay and south Puget Sound are not counted as shore.
    • Quiet: zones around highways6, rail lines5 and airports7, the number of people living within 8 km1,2, and average wind from airport weather stations8,9. Station coverage is thin in Washington, Utah and Wyoming.
    • Schools are grade levels above or below the national average for 2009–1910, from the schools in the neighborhood’s own school district11: the nearest three to five public schools with test data in the district that covers home (elementary district where a state has them), closer ones counting more. Charter schools are left out of this because they have no attendance area. Until November 2026 this was every school within 3 km, regardless of district; that blurred district lines, especially in exurbs. District boundaries are the Census Bureau’s 2025 school district maps. Attendance zones inside a district are not public, so check a specific address with the district. The 2025 figures12 are estimated for Colorado from its state tests13, and Oregon has none.
    • The four optional criteria (added November 2026). Affordability: the typical home value, cheapest best. Learning growth: how fast students in the same district schools gain ground each year compared with the U.S. average (the Stanford Education Data Archive’s grade-to-grade growth, 2009–19); unlike Schools it reflects the schools more than who lives nearby. Hands-on K–8: public and charter Montessori, Waldorf-method, EL Education and IB Primary Years schools, plus progressive or project-based option schools, with closer schools counting more (a school 6 km away counts about a third as much as one next door). The list combines the Metro Neighborhood Atlas schools, every public school with Montessori, Waldorf or Expeditionary in its name, the Alliance for Public Waldorf Education member list, and a hand-picked list of EL Education and progressive schools; IB Primary Years schools are included only in the six metros, so IB-heavy areas elsewhere are underrated. Play-based pre-K: Montessori, Waldorf, Reggio-inspired and nature-based programs from the federal private school list, OpenStreetMap and the Metro Neighborhood Atlas’s licensing-list programs, closer ones counting more. Outside the six metros this finds roughly half of such programs (in Colorado, 64 of the 115 Montessori centres on the state licensing list), so treat small differences as noise. Private schools count for pre-K but not for K–8. Tree cover (added November 17): the share of land under tree canopy within about 5 km of home, from the U.S. Forest Service’s 2023 Tree Canopy Cover map at about 500 m detail, with lakes and sea left out. Open pine forest reads lower than it feels: Mammoth Lakes is about 29%, Flagstaff 24%, Nevada City 49%, Reno 6%.
    • Climate: county projections of days at or above 95°F and of dry spells by the 2050s1, wildfire hazard14 scaled by its projected change15, and ozone and fine-particle readings for 2019–2516. The heat figure is moved from the county to each neighborhood’s own elevation and distance from the coast, and is rough in California’s interior valleys.
    • Walkable core: town centres from the atlas’s town-centre rule (a downtown needs shops and restaurants with civic offices alongside; a main street or corner needs a tight street grid17 or a neighborhood where at least a third of homes pre-date 195018) count as cores where the national walkability index17 is at least 10 of 20. A core’s size is the number of such neighborhoods within 2 km. Access is full within 5 km of a core and falls to nothing at 15 km (straight-line), multiplied by a size factor that runs from the Small-core credit setting in Weights (60% to start) for a single neighborhood up to 1 for 16 or more; the best core counts. Unlike the other criteria it is shown as access out of 100, not a percentile. Until October 10, 2026 this criterion was plain walkability (half the national index, half distance to a town centre).
    • Home value is Zillow’s neighborhood figure where one exists, otherwise the ZIP code’s19,20,21. Neighborhood names come from the same sources.
    • Airport: the nearest airport7 on a hand-checked list of those with year-round daily airline service. Distance is a straight line, so ferries and mountain passes are not accounted for except on the Olympic Peninsula.
    • Maps are drawn on OpenStreetMap base maps22; neighborhood outlines are the census tract boundaries1, simplified.

    References

    1. Climate Mapping for Resilience and Adaptation (CMRA). Census tract assessment data: 2010 tract boundaries and populations, projected days at or above 95°F and consecutive dry days (LOCA downscaling, RCP 8.5, mid-century), and tract-average wildfire hazard.
    2. U.S. Census Bureau. Centers of Population, 2010 Census, tracts and block groups.
    3. PRISM Climate Group, Oregon State University. PRISM 4 km elevation grid, as packaged in the R package fields.
    4. Browning, M. H. E. M., Rigolon, A., et al. (2022). The PAD-US-AR dataset: Measuring accessible and recreational parks in the contiguous United States. Scientific Data 9.
    5. U.S. Census Bureau. TIGER/Line Shapefiles, 2025: coastline and rail lines.
    6. Natural Earth. 1:10m roads, North America supplement.
    7. OurAirports. Airport locations and types.
    8. Western Regional Climate Center. Average wind speeds by station, 1996–2006.
    9. NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information. Comparative Climatic Data: mean wind speed, through 2018.
    10. Reardon, S. F., et al. (2024). Stanford Education Data Archive, version 5.0: school and district test-score estimates, 2009–2019 (technical documentation).
    11. National Center for Education Statistics. EDGE school geocodes, public schools 2022–23.
    12. Stanford Education Data Archive. SEDA 2025: school estimates for 2022–2025 and district estimates for 2024–25.
    13. Colorado Department of Education. CMAS data and results, 2019 and spring 2025.
    14. USDA Forest Service. Wildfire Hazard Potential for the United States (270 m), as averaged by census tract in the CMRA data.
    15. Federal Emergency Management Agency. National Risk Index: Future Risk Index, December 2024 (technical documentation, archived copy): projected mid-century change in wildfire and drought, by county.
    16. U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. Air Quality System (AirData): annual summaries by monitor, 2019–2025, for ozone and PM2.5.
    17. U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (2021). Smart Location Database, version 3.0, including the National Walkability Index, jobs by sector and street-intersection density (technical documentation).
    18. U.S. Census Bureau. American Community Survey, 2015–2019 five-year estimates, table B25034 (year structure built), by block group.
    19. Zillow Research. Zillow Home Value Index: single-family homes, ZIP-code and neighborhood series, to August 2026.
    20. Zillow. Neighborhood boundaries, 2017 release.
    21. OpenDataDE. State ZIP code GeoJSON: Census ZIP Code Tabulation Areas, 2010.
